questions.stem:
Choose the correct sentence:
A. I have seen this film yesterday.
B. I saw this film yesterday.
C. I was seeing this film yesterday.
D. I have been seeing this film yesterday.

options.option_text: A (incorrect: 'have seen' = present perfect; cannot be used with 'yesterday', a specific past time)
B (correct: simple past is used for completed actions at a specific past time; 'yesterday' requires simple past ✓)
C (incorrect: 'was seeing' = past continuous, used for an ongoing action, not completed viewing)
D (incorrect: 'have been seeing' = present perfect continuous; cannot be used with 'yesterday')

questions.explanation: B is correct. Rule: Present Perfect (have/has + V3) CANNOT be used with specific past time words: yesterday, ago, last night, in 2020, etc. Only Simple Past tense is used with definite past time. 'I saw this film yesterday' ✓. Compare: 'I have seen this film before' (no specific time = ✓).

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'By the time the rescue team arrived, the flood ______ the entire village.'

options.option_text: flooded (simple past — doesn't show that the flooding happened BEFORE rescue team arrival)
had flooded (correct: past perfect = action completed before another past action; flooding happened before rescue team arrived ✓)
has flooded (present perfect — wrong tense for past reference)
was flooding (past continuous = ongoing, not completed before arrival)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Past Perfect (had + V3) is used for an action completed BEFORE another past action. 'By the time the rescue team arrived (past event)... the flood HAD FLOODED (earlier past event).' Trigger: 'By the time + past simple' signals past perfect in the main clause.

questions.stem: Which tense is used in: 'She will have completed the project by Friday.'?

options.option_text: Future Simple (will + V1 — simple future, not 'will have + V3')
Future Perfect (correct: will have + V3 = future perfect; expresses a future action completed before a specific future time ✓)
Future Continuous (will be + V1-ing — not 'will have + V3')
Future Perfect Continuous (will have been + V1-ing — not used here)

questions.explanation: B is correct. FUTURE PERFECT = will have + V3. Used to express an action that will be completed before a specific future time or another future event. 'She will have completed the project BY FRIDAY.' Signal words: by + future time (by tomorrow, by noon, by next week).

questions.stem:
Identify the incorrect sentence regarding tense:
A. She has lived here for ten years.
B. He has gone to the market an hour ago.
C. They had eaten before I arrived.
D. We will be travelling all night.

options.option_text: A (correct: 'has lived for ten years' = present perfect for an ongoing situation ✓)
B (incorrect: 'has gone...an hour ago' — present perfect cannot be used with specific past time 'an hour ago' → should be 'went' ✓)
C (correct: past perfect for earlier past action ✓)
D (correct: future continuous for ongoing future action ✓)

questions.explanation: B is the incorrect sentence. 'Has gone...an hour ago' violates the rule that present perfect cannot be used with specific past time expressions. 'An hour ago' specifies a past time → use Simple Past: 'He WENT to the market an hour ago.' A, C, and D are all grammatically correct.

questions.stem: Choose the correct tense: 'The children ______ (play) in the garden when it started to rain.'

options.option_text: played (simple past — doesn't express the ongoing background activity when rain started)
were playing (correct: past continuous for an ongoing background action interrupted by a sudden event (simple past) ✓)
had played (past perfect — implies completed action, not interrupted one)
have been playing (present perfect continuous — wrong tense for past narrative)

questions.explanation: B is correct. PAST CONTINUOUS (was/were + V-ing) is used for an ongoing background action interrupted by a shorter action (simple past). Pattern: '...were playing (ongoing)... WHEN it started to rain (interruption).' The keyword 'when' signals the interruption.

questions.stem:
Select the correct sentence:
A. I am knowing the answer.
B. I know the answer.
C. I am knowing the answer now.
D. I have been knowing the answer.

options.option_text: A (incorrect: 'know' is a stative verb — doesn't take continuous form)
B (correct: stative verbs (know, believe, love, hate, understand, want, seem) don't use continuous form ✓)
C (same error as A — 'knowing' is wrong even with 'now')
D (same error — 'have been knowing' is incorrect for stative verb)

questions.explanation: B is correct. STATIVE VERBS express states (not actions) and cannot be used in continuous tenses. Common stative verbs: know, believe, understand, love, hate, want, need, have (possess), seem, belong, contain, mean, prefer, remember. 'I know (NOT I am knowing).' This is a very frequently tested error type.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the Present Perfect Continuous tense correctly?

options.option_text: She has been wait for two hours. (wrong: should be 'waiting' not 'wait')
I have been studying since morning. (correct: have been + V-ing + 'since' = present perfect continuous; action started in past and continues now ✓)
He has been gone to the market. (wrong: 'gone' is not continuous — 'has been going' or 'has gone')
They have been finished the work. (wrong: 'finished' — should use present perfect: 'have finished')

questions.explanation: B is correct. Present Perfect Continuous = have/has been + V-ing. Used for: (1) actions that started in the past and continue now, (2) ongoing recently completed actions with visible effects. Trigger words: since (specific time), for (duration). 'I have been studying since morning' = started this morning, still ongoing.

questions.stem: Complete the conditional: 'If it ______ tomorrow, we will cancel the trip.'

options.option_text: rains (correct: Type 1 conditional (real/possible): 'If + present simple, will + V1' ✓)
rained (Type 2 conditional: 'If + past simple, would + V1' — would, not will)
will rain (wrong: don't use 'will' in the 'if' clause of conditional sentences)
had rained (Type 3 conditional for impossible past; wrong here)

questions.explanation: A is correct. TYPE 1 CONDITIONAL (real possibility): If + present simple (rains), WILL + base verb (will cancel). Never use 'will' in the 'if' clause. Type 2 (hypothetical): If + past simple, WOULD + base. Type 3 (impossible past): If + past perfect (had rained), WOULD HAVE + V3.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'The sun ______ in the east.'

options.option_text: rises (correct: for permanent/scientific/habitual truths, use Simple Present ✓)
is rising (present continuous = ongoing right now; not for permanent facts)
has risen (present perfect = recent past, not permanent truth)
rose (simple past = specific past event, not habitual/permanent truth)

questions.explanation: A is correct. SIMPLE PRESENT is used for: (1) permanent truths / scientific facts ('The sun rises in the east'); (2) habitual actions ('He exercises daily'); (3) definitions ('Water boils at 100°C'). Not present continuous, which describes an action happening right now.

questions.stem:
Select the sentence with CORRECT use of the Simple Past vs Past Perfect:
A. When I reached the station, the train already left.
B. When I reached the station, the train had already left.
C. When I had reached the station, the train left.
D. When I reached the station, the train was already left.

options.option_text: A (wrong: 'left' in simple past doesn't show it happened before reaching — need past perfect)
B (correct: train departure (past perfect: had left) happened before I reached (simple past: reached) ✓)
C (wrong: reversed — 'had reached' makes arrival the earlier event, but train 'left' in simple past doesn't clarify sequence)
D ('was already left' is wrong — not a valid construction)

questions.explanation: B is correct. When two past events occur, the EARLIER one uses Past Perfect (had + V3), and the LATER one uses Simple Past. Sequence: train left (earlier) → I reached (later). 'When I REACHED the station (later), the train HAD ALREADY LEFT (earlier).' Note: 'already' reinforces the past perfect.
